text: Natalia sold clips to forty-eight friends in April, and half as many in May. How many altogether?
Seventy-two. A ten-year-old can do that.
Now watch a half-billion-number model try.
Half of forty-eight is... thirty-four?! Eighty-two? Oh no.
Today we make it better, with nothing but a rule that checks the final number. And you’ll learn how to judge what really changed.
Teach Qwen word problems. Episode two.
The whole project is seven stages, and Tiny is going to walk them for us.
Set up. A smoke test. A baseline. Then the long part: training, roughly an hour.
Then curves, a second test, and saving the model. Got it.
Those times are estimates, not measurements. Answers get longer as it learns, and longer answers take longer to write.
Stage one is the most skipped, and the most important: the baseline.
Can’t I just train it, and see if it’s good?
Good compared with what? Scientists don’t test a medicine without a control group. Your control group is the untrained model.
Two hundred test questions, two numbers. Accuracy: the right number, inside the answer tags. And format rate: did it use the exact shape?
Write both down before training. Got it.
Here’s a subtle catch. Look at this answer.
Forty-eight plus twenty-four, seventy-two. That’s right!
The maths is right. But there are no answer tags, so our accuracy counts it as wrong.
Wait, what? It got it right, and it scores zero?
On purpose. It matches the training reward. But it means part of any improvement might be format alone. Keep that in mind.
Then the real run. Every five steps, you get a line like this. It looks scary. It isn’t.
Format reward: half a point at most. Hope for it to rise, often early and fast.
Correctness: one at most. Hope for a slow, noisy drift upward.
And mean length is how long the answers are?
In tokens. Just watch it doesn’t slam into the limit of two hundred and fifty-six.
This one is the fraction of groups where all eight answers scored the same. Those teach nothing, so it shouldn’t sit near one.
And the last one is the leash: small, and slowly rising.
And expect noise. Each step only sees two questions.
So one easy question makes a step look brilliant, and the next one looks awful?
Exactly. So judge the trend over twenty or thirty steps. A healthy run often looks something like this. An example, not a promise.
Format climbs first, because tags are easy. Correctness follows, slowly.
Training ends, and you test again. Say the format rate went up a lot, but accuracy only went up a little.
Did the run fail?
Pause, and have a guess.
A. Honestly? It learned the tags, not the maths. That’s a fail.
Harsh! It’s B. That’s normal for two hundred and fifty steps on a model this small.
Even the DeepSeek-R1 team found small models gain more from copying a big model’s reasoning than from this kind of training alone. So set your hopes honestly.
Then the most underrated step: read some real answers. Numbers tell you how much changed. Answers tell you what changed.
Is the thinking real, or just filler?
Is the arithmetic right? Small models love to set it up perfectly, then miss forty-eight divided by two.
Did it game the format? An almost empty think block still earns the format reward.
And did it get cut off, mid-sentence?
Finally, save it. Merge the add-on into the model, and upload it, private by default. Colab deletes everything when the session ends.
And then write it up?
Five lines. Setup. Before and after. One sentence per curve. One answer that improved, and one that didn’t. And the one knob you’d change next.
Quick recap.
Measure a baseline first. It’s your control group.
Judge the trend over many steps, not single jumps.
And read real answers, then report what happened honestly.
So your run is done, and your curves are on screen.
All nine of them.
Nine plots?! Which ones do I actually look at? And how do I know if my run is healthy, or just looks healthy?
